Distinguished delegates, civil society organizations stand united in urging ambitious and inclusive action to tackle desertification, land degradation, and drought. The meaningful inclusion of all rights holders, women, youth, indigenous people, local communities, is essential to shaping policies that effectively advance sustainable land management and restoration. Today, we have three demands. First, we call on parties to develop and implement policies and governance frameworks that actively end support for harmful activities such as land-degrading agriculture, extractive industries and deforestation. Promote agroecological and agroforestry approaches. Support locally led initiatives and traditional knowledge on sustainable land use, conservation and restoration. Promote environmental education focused on youth and children. Support peace efforts to end conflicts across the world, which hinder attempts to tackle DLDD. Those policies are central to building drought resilience, restoring ecosystems, ensuring sustainable use and fostering healthy food systems. Second, provide accessible funding through innovative mechanisms tailored to the needs of rights holders and grassroots organizations, which empower locally-led action, knowledge exchange, and capacity building. Funding should be made available without political impediments or relying on intermediaries. Finally, we call on parties to strengthen CSO participation for more meaningful engagement including allowing CSOs as silent observers in contact groups, providing financial support for translation services and capacity building, among others. Critical times require critical actions. As we look towards COP17, let us carry a collective resolve to protect the land that sustain us, honor the wisdom and rights of its stewards, and forge a path that secures dignity and opportunity for all. Thank you.

Thank you, Chair, distinguished guests. Today, as COP16 comes to a close, we stand united in our call for action to combat desertification, land degradation, and drought. As a highlight from my engagement here through organizing as the UNCCD Youth Caucus, allow me to highlight the success of the fourth youth forum in shaping the declaration on youth engagement as youth worldwide face barriers to participating fully in governance, policy making, and sustainable entrepreneurship. Our shared legacy is at risk without action. Together we can create a future where land degradation is a thing of the past, as land thrives as a foundation for life. Youth are not just hope for the future, we are driving change today. With that in mind, we would like to call upon the parties as follows upon decisions for COP16.2. Advance youth-focused policies by promoting equitable land rights, particularly for marginalized groups like young women, children, refugees, indigenous communities, while fostering youth collaboration across the Rio Conventions to amplify advocacy. Ensure gender inclusion by guaranteeing land tenure for women to promote equitable land access and mean participation of young people in agri-food system policy making. Institutionalize youth participation in land governance and decision-making processes, as well as in developing and implementing DLDD policies and accountability frameworks by supporting the implementation of the UNCCD Youth Engagement Strategy. Provide accessible and flexible funding for youth-led initiatives while prioritizing finance support for youth, women, and children, particularly in the Global South and conflict-affected areas to advance ecosystems restoration aligned with goals of peace, security, and resilience. Invest in green jobs while improving existing ones by ensuring fair wages and safe working conditions in sectors like agriculture and forestry. Provide training for youth on the science policy interface to improve their understanding and application of sustainable land management and resilience building strategies. And also create inclusive spaces where young people can share best practices while fostering international and intergenerational collaboration to share and replicate effective DLD solutions in integrating indigenous knowledge with scientific research. In closing, the intentionality of the Convention to centre youth engagement was fully felt for us when the Parties requested the Secretariat for a youth engagement strategy. And since then, we the young people have worked very closely with various stakeholders to respond. The UNCCD Youth Engagement Strategy is not just a document, it's a roadmap, a call to action, and a testament to the belief that young people are not only stakeholders but catalysts for transformation in combating desertification, land degradation, and drought, as it seeks to bridge this gap by embedding youth voices and actions into the very fabric of their conventions, policies, and programs. We the youth of the world stand united for land, calling upon the global community to listen, engage and act. This is our legacy, our future. Let us protect it together. Thank you.

We Indigenous peoples are grateful to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the UNCCD Secretariat for this historic gathering of Indigenous peoples from the seven socio-cultural regions. Today, history has been made. With the support of all of the parties of this convention, the CSO and the Secretariat, an Indigenous Peoples' Caucus and a Local Communities' Caucus have been established, a shared legacy that we can all be proud of. As Indigenous peoples and rights holders, we are committed to preserving our common home, our Mother Earth. something we can now champion through our new caucus. We called on you to support us and you have answered our call. We thank you. But there is still further work to do to tackle the growing threat of land degradation and Indigenous peoples are here to help overcome this global challenge. So as we stated in our declaration, we urge the parties to take additional action including to ensure and promote full effective respect for our rights, including the rights to land tenure, governance, and management of our territories as set forth under the UNDRIP. We call for our Indigenous people's knowledge, innovation, sciences, technologies, and values to be ethically and equitably incorporated into the implementation and monitoring of UNCCD With respect to free, prior and informed consent, our knowledge should be deemed equal to Western sciences and technologies. We urge you to provide us with a permanent seat on the Committee on Science and Technology. We call for the establishment of direct funding mechanisms that are equitable, accessible, non-discriminatory, flexible and responsive to our priorities without political impediments and ensure a seat for Indigenous peoples on the Riyadh Action Agenda and Riyadh Drought Resilience Partnerships Fund. We, Indigenous peoples, stand ready to work constructively with the parties, the secretariat and COP presidency to ensure that our solutions contribute to the well-being of humanity and our planet. We leave this space with the hope that our voices be heard and included as essential pillars for building a sustainable future. Boda wan.
